About a month ago /u/HomerSimpson (pbuh) brought to my attention to case of 8chan, where the owner lost control of his website and company due to an untrustworthy registrar who siezed control of the domain after a sustained attack and pressure from external sources. More info here. I love the .mg domain, it's unique and short but there is the potential that it could face the same problems as 8chan.co.

To mitigate this potential problem we purchased an additional domain, ioIMG.com, .com domains are operated by the American company Verisign which likely has much stronger intellectual property protections than the Madagascar run .mg domain.

ioIMG is just an alternative, the site uses the same databases and servers, the only difference between these two sites is the name. If you have an account on sli.mg it is accessible from the alternate domain.

This also means that if Sli.mg is blocked at your place of work or is not resolving properly for whatever reason just replace it with ioIMG.com and it will work.

e.g. https://sli.mg/4Wq4sr.png

change to

https://ioimg.com/4Wq4sr.png

Additionally we have added to our list of features to develop both chrome and firefox extensions which will automatically redirect you if you have problems accessing sli.mg regularly.

Take any big commonly used app on Linux Desktops today, be it GIMP, Transmission, Inkscape, Evince, etc. or hundreds of others in the KDE world like Kate, K3b, KDevelop, etc.: they are either developed using C/GTK+ or C++/Qt, why don't we have any Java apps? After all Write once run anywhere (wora) was the promise of Java.

Hell, we even have the .NET app called Pinta in the ubuntu repos. Is Java really that bad? With just one single codebase of Swing/SWT/JavaFX, you can scale all the GNOME + KDE + Windows worlds. Isn't that motivation enough for developers to start developing in Java for Linux desktops?
Why didn't the Java WORA model work that well on Linux Desktops?

I am by no means an expert, so take my speculation below with a heap of salt.

I suspect it is a combination of factors:

I've noticed a lot of people in the linux/unix community aren't particularly infatuated with OOP-style programming. They tend to come from more of a C background, so C++ is probably less of a jump for them. They'll use OOP as a tool, but not as religious doctrine, and C++ allows for that kind of flexibility more easily.

I also suspect there is a general and deserved distrust of Oracle. We don't know what they will do next, and Oracle has done some really sleazy stuff in the past. Nobody wants to get the rug pulled out from under them.

Lastly, something that runs on the JVM can't be as fast as something that runs natively. For a lot of programs, this probably isn't a problem, but if you're writing for speed, it could be.

Edit: I forgot to mention, Java is popular on the server-side.

They tend to come from more of a C background, so C++ is probably less of a jump for them.

Yeah, sure. But programming in Java is so much easier, and I'm not just talking about OOP here. Firstly, you don't have to worry about free() and alloc() as you do in C/C++. Most importantly, Java syntax is derived from C and C++, so a programmer in these languages should naturally feel at home in Java. The Java garbage collector does that for you automatically. Secondly, you just have to build one jar and that runs on all the platforms - Linux, Mac and Windows. In C/C++, you have to build and test and keep testing for a while on all three platforms before you get some amount of confidence.

I also suspect there is a general and deserved distrust of Oracle.

Again, Oracle is a Troll, but Java is pure FOSS. The OpenJDK project is different than Oracle and so is the Java Community Process (JCP) that is in control of the Java technology.

Lastly, something that runs on the JVM can't be as fast as something that runs natively. For a lot of programs, this probably isn't a problem, but if you're writing for speed, it could be.

Like you said, for about 90% of userland GUI apps, the difference is not noticeable by the user. If the user gets the same experience while at the same time easing the life of programmer, then why not go for Java?

I'm not overly anti-Java myself, I do some programming in Java. I'm just guessing at the reasons Java has never really took off in Linux desktop land.

Taking your points one by one:

  1. A lot of C/C++ programmers are really anal about wanting full and direct control of their memory allocation and frees. Personally, I'm usually happy having something else manage it. I personally think C++'s RAII model is pretty awesome, but a lot of people would prefer to write C in C++, which C++ will allow them to do. I personally think there are some situations where C-style programming makes sense, but I like to avoid it when possible. But, I'm not everyone. I would say there is a different culture between C/C++ programmers and Java programmers.

  2. Fair point. However, OpenJDK doesn't really seem to be working as well as Oracle's JDK for some things ATM. This could probably change in the future, but that's the state things are in right now. For example, using OpenJDK with intellij is a major PITA.

  3. I think there is an "optimization" culture in the linux/unix community, and the open source community in general. Maybe sometimes to its detriment, but often for the good. A lot of programmers like implementing some algorithm that will speed things up by 0.5%. Also, in situations where you are dealing with a slow CPU and low memory, optimized native programs become a lot more enticing.

I want to emphasize that I think no one of these things is a reason Java hasn't really taken off in linux. I think it's a combination of these factors, and probably a few more. I'm speculating.
JAVA GUIs are really, really inefficient and slow. At least, that's been my experience.

If you look at the history of Linux or FreeBSD, those too were written in litigations! When a thing gets popular, companies play the ego battle and try to assert their rights over it, it has almost become a norm in the valley. SCO tried to do the same with Linux and BSDI tried to hold claim over FreeBSD, but today nobody remembers them. All we know are the Linux and FreeBSD communities. Few decades later, nobody will remember Oracle or Goolge firms, but people will remember Java and Android communities. So, don't worry about that too much.

The codebase/ development is not pretty, and there is perl, python, ruby, and a half dozen other languages that do things you would have "had to" use java for, but with less headaches.

If you think about it, perl, python and ruby are interpreted languages, so their performance will never match that of Java. Granted that performance is not always the priority, in fact, I tend to use a lot of python and php myself especially when it comes to web. But the point is that language is just a tool and there is a right tool for every job. And for some jobs, the right tool might be Java.
